documentation.range:
Remora remora occurs worldwide in tropical and sub-tropical waters. In the western Atlantic it is known from Nova Scotia, Canada to Argentina, including the Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean Sea and Trinidade Island (Robins and Ray 1986, Collette 2002, Simon et al. 2013). In the eastern Atlantic it is known from Iceland, the North Sea, throughout the Mediterranean Sea, and along West Africa to South Africa (Lachner 1986, Appleby 1999). In the Indo-Pacific it is known along East Africa, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, southern Japan, Australia, New Zealand and Norfolk Island, and the Hawaiian Islands (Masuda et al. 1984, Francis 1993). In the eastern Pacific it is known from San Francisco, California (USA) south along Central and South America to Chile (Eschmeyer et al. 1983). Its depth range is 1-100 m, but this also is dependent upon the depth that the host reaches.

There are records from the Gulf of Mexico, as this species was taken off a sailfish (Springer 1961) and another was taken off Texas (Bowling and Sunley 1996).
documentation.population: Remora remora is common worldwide (Heemstra 1986). Its occurrence is dependent on the occurrence of suitable host species.
documentation.habitats: This pelagic, offshore species is usually associated with sharks, but also attaches itself to other large fishes, sea turtles and even ships. Sometimes it is free-swimming (Cressey and Lachner 1970). Maximum size to 62 cm (SL), but reported to 86 cm (TL) (Claro 1994). It feeds on parasitic copepods (Cressey and Lachner 1970).Younger Remora remora are more active as parasite pickers.
documentation.threats: There are no known major threats.
documentation.measures: There are no species-specific conservation measures.
documentation.use_trade: Remora remora is often harvested for food in the Eastern Central Atlantic, especially in Ghana and Senegal, in which it is marketed dried-salted and smoked [Collette ECA FAO in prep].
documentation.rationale: Remora remora is widely distributed and common where it is usually associated with sharks, but also attaches itself to other large fishes, sea turtles and even ships. There are no known major threats, therefore, it is listed as Least Concern.
